source.title: A Geometric Look at Double Descent Risk: Volumes, Singularities, and Distinguishabilities

record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps fitted feature dimension in synthetic ridge regression and reports test-risk curves, testing double descent in a different model class and setup from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The paper also derives model-volume and MDL results for linear regression and statistical lattices. These are not test-error measurements; the lattice MDL trend is recorded separately as a related finding. The paper cites other studies' results on regularization and more data; those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own sweep of fitted feature dimension D (1 to 2500) in synthetic ridge regression at three sample sizes and three ridge strengths. It reports test-risk curves (Fig. 3) bearing on V4 (double descent outside deep nets) and V6 (dependence on regularization). Most of the paper is MDL/model-volume theory, which is not a risk measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely correct. The authors argue that the log model-volume term (channel-capacity saturation plus ball/simplex volume shrinking with D) offsets the O(D) AIC/BIC penalty, so test error need not explode when D far exceeds N. Their ridge experiments show a peak at N = D under weak regularization, saturation at large D, a rightward peak shift with N, and suppression or elimination of the peak under stronger ridge.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic isotropic linear regression with a sweep over fitted feature dimension and ridge penalty, rather than deep-network size, epoch, or training-sample interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-risk curve changes with ridge parameter alpha; the authors also report that the peak shifts right as sample size N increases.

fits_no_version.finding: For fully observable statistical lattice models, the derived MDL expression first rises and then falls with dimension D. This is driven by a 1/(D-1)! simplex-volume term and is illustrated on toy values in Fig. 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MDL code length for statistical lattice models shows a rise-then-fall trend with dimension, without a measured test-risk curve.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ridge experiments the test-risk peak coincides with the peak of the squared norm of beta, and both scale with alpha (Fig. 3, bottom row).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ridge regression the double-descent risk peak coincides with a peak in coefficient norm at the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The empirical risk values are shown in plots without numerical values or reported uncertainty. The risk experiment is limited to synthetic isotropic regression with fixed Gaussian noise and a small set of ridge parameters. The more-data claim is not directly established by a stated fixed-dimension comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical test-error values were available in the text; Figure 3 values are recorded as figure only. Other theoretical model-volume bounds were not entered as risk rows.

untested.parts: No sweep over epochs or training time.
The peak is said to shift right with N, and the authors infer more data could hurt. No test error at fixed D across N is reported numerically or stated explicitly.
No test of a single complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label noise is fixed (noise N(0,1), fixed SNR). No multiple peaks are examined. Whether alpha is optimally tuned is not examined.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count.
Only isotropic Gaussian linear ridge regression is tested empirically; other model classes are covered by theory only.

missing.what: Coefficient-norm (squared norm of beta) curves whose peak coincides with the test-risk peak and depends on alpha
Statement that the double-descent peak shifts right with increasing N, with the authors' inference that more data can hurt at fixed model size

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The empirical evidence is figure-only, with a single fixed seed, 10-fold CV and no uncertainty reported. The reader's V6 limits_scope label for alpha = 10^0 was removed: a partial reduction under moderate ridge is consistent with V6, not a qualification of it. V3 was moved to untested because the rows cannot show error rising with N at fixed D.

versions.untested_parts: The empirical models are ridge regression, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
The paper reports that the peak shifts with sample size, but does not explicitly compare test error at a fixed model size near the interpolation threshold to establish that adding samples raises it.
The empirical risk sweep is for isotropic linear regression; the paper does not test risk curves across a range of model classes.
The paper proposes a geometric account but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Regularization strength is varied, but label noise or variance is not swept, multiple or triple peaks are not tested, and the paper does not report an optimally tuned regularizer.
The paper does not re-express the empirical second descent using an effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Isotropic linear ridge regression, alpha = 10^-2, N = 300/600/900
relationships.reason: Per the text, test error peaks at N = D and then falls and saturates as D grows past N (r1-r3). Figure only, single fixed seed.
relationships.display_finding: Test error peaked at N=D, then fell and saturated as D grew beyond N in experiments using a single fixed seed.

relationships.condition: Isotropic linear ridge regression with stronger ridge, alpha = 10^0 and 10^2
relationships.reason: The peak is progressively reduced and, per the text, can be completely eliminated, so the double-descent shape depends on the ridge penalty (r4-r9).
relationships.display_finding: Increasing the ridge penalty through α = 10⁰ and 10² progressively reduced the peak and could eliminate it completely.

relationships.condition: Isotropic linear ridge regression, alpha from 10^-2 to 10^2
relationships.reason: There is a peak under weak ridge (r1-r3), a gradual reduction (r4-r6) and complete elimination under strong ridge (r7-r9). This matches regularization removing the peak, though optimality of alpha is not shown.
relationships.display_finding: Across α from 10^-2 to 10^2, the peak weakened and then disappeared under strong ridge.
